title: The Septic Child
subtitle: 6-year-old with fever, hypotension and delayed capillary refill
stem: Paediatric emergency, 11:20 pm. Meera, 6 years, is carried in by her father. Fever for three days, now very sleepy. You are the emergency nurse; the doctor is two beds away.
parent: "She had fever and loose motions since Thursday. The medical shop gave her syrup. Today she stopped drinking, passed urine only once, and since evening she just wants to sleep. Her hands are so cold."

vitals.note: Lethargic, opens eyes to voice, weak cry. Mottled knees, cold hands and feet to the wrists, peripheral pulses weak, central pulses present. No recessions. Dry lips. Hypotension threshold for 6 years = 70 + (2 × 6) = 82 mmHg systolic.

options.text: Unstable — breathing: respiratory distress, RR 32 is fast
options.outcome: You give oxygen and set up a nebuliser. Her hands grow colder; CRT 5 s.
options.note: The rate is up, but there is no increased effort; this is the breathing of acidosis and fever, not a lung problem. The abnormal sides are appearance and circulation.

options.text: Unstable, life-threatening — circulation: shock
options.outcome: You call the doctor over and move her to the resuscitation bay.
options.note: Mottled, pale skin with a lethargic, poorly interacting child is shock until proved otherwise, and the abnormal appearance tells you the brain is already under-perfused: this is decompensated, not early.

options.text: Unstable — neurological: lethargy with fever means meningitis
options.outcome: You start preparing a lumbar puncture tray. Meanwhile CRT is 5 s and HR 158.
options.note: Lethargy with normal circulation would point to a primary brain problem. Here the skin is mottled and cold: the brain is lethargic because of shock. Treat the shock; look for the source after.

options.text: Stable — dehydrated; oral rehydration salts and observe
options.outcome: She is given ORS and does not drink it. Twenty minutes later she responds only to pain; CRT 5 s.
options.note: Dehydration that produces mottling, CRT 4 s and lethargy is hypovolaemic shock and needs IV fluid now. ORS Plan A/B is for a child who is alert and can drink.

decisions.title: Intervention

options.text: Full history and head-to-toe examination to find the source of infection
options.outcome: Ten minutes into the history and examination she still has no IV line. CRT 5 s, HR 160.
options.note: Source-finding is for after resuscitation. In the first five minutes the only question is: oxygen, access, glucose.

options.text: Oxygen, monitoring, two IV lines (IO if needed), glucose, blood culture, 20 mL/kg isotonic bolus by push–pull, antibiotics within the hour
options.outcome: Oxygen on, monitored. Two IV lines in 4 minutes; culture sent; glucose 3.1 mmol/L treated with 10 % dextrose 2 mL/kg. The first 20 mL/kg bolus goes in over 8 minutes by push–pull and the antibiotic at 25 minutes. Hands slightly warmer: HR 142, BP 82/44, CRT 3 s.
options.note: Oxygen even with SpO₂ 96 % (shock is a delivery problem), monitoring, access within 5 minutes with IO as the fallback, glucose (hypoglycaemia is common and fatal), culture before antibiotics but antibiotics never delayed for a culture.

options.text: Paracetamol for the fever and a cold sponge; shock will improve once the temperature falls
options.outcome: The cold sponge makes her shiver and the mottling spreads up her legs. CRT 5 s, HR 160.
options.note: The fever is not causing the shock. A cold sponge worsens peripheral vasoconstriction. Antipyretics can come after the bolus.

options.text: Insert a urinary catheter first to measure output
options.outcome: The catheter takes 10 minutes. There is still no IV line; CRT 5 s.
options.note: Urine output is a useful trend, but it is not a first-five-minutes action and it is not access. Oxygen, IV/IO, glucose, fluid.

options.text: Start IV fluids: 20 mL/kg over one hour on the infusion pump
options.outcome: The pump runs at 400 mL/h. Thirty minutes in she is still mottled, BP 76/40, now responding only to pain.
options.note: Right volume, wrong speed. A bolus in shock is given over 5–10 minutes; over an hour it is maintenance, and she stays in shock for an hour.

decisions.key: Oxygen, monitoring, IV/IO access within 5 minutes, bedside glucose, blood culture, a 10–20 mL/kg isotonic crystalloid bolus pushed over 5–10 minutes (push–pull) with reassessment after each bolus, and antibiotics within the hour.

decisions.title: Reassessment
decisions.label: Your reassessment
decisions.prompt: After two boluses (40 mL/kg) and the antibiotic: HR 140, BP 80/42, CRT 3 s, still cold to the wrists and lethargic; chest clear, liver 1 cm. Reassess her: what is happening, and what do you do now?

opts.v: After each bolus: HR, BP, CRT, limb temperature, mental status
Third and fourth boluses until the BP is normal
Look for fluid overload: crackles, liver size, SpO₂, work of breathing
Recheck glucose; send a blood gas and lactate
Fluid-refractory cold shock: tell the doctor and prepare adrenaline (a peripheral line is acceptable)
Furosemide — she has had 800 mL
Measure urine output
Wait for a central line before starting any infusion

options.text: After each bolus: HR, BP, CRT, limb temperature, mental status; Look for fluid overload: crackles, liver size, SpO₂, work of breathing; Fluid-refractory cold shock: tell the doctor and prepare adrenaline (a peripheral line is acceptable)
options.outcome: Adrenaline at 0.1 microgram/kg/min through the peripheral line. Warm to the elbows, HR 128, BP 92/50, CRT 2 s, alert. She passes 60 mL of urine.
options.note: Persistent shock after 40–60 mL/kg is fluid-refractory. Reassess after every bolus, look for overload, and in cold shock start adrenaline — peripherally if needed.

options.text: Some correct elements, nothing unsafe (partial)
options.outcome: Part of the picture is missed; 20 minutes pass before the team decides on adrenaline. BP 76/40, CRT 4 s.

options.text: Third and fourth boluses until the BP is normal
options.outcome: After the fourth bolus: crackles at both bases, liver 3 cm, RR 40, SpO₂ 92 %.

options.text: Furosemide — she has had 800 mL
options.outcome: Furosemide given. BP falls to 70/36, CRT 5 s, she responds only to pain.

options.text: Wait for a central line before starting any infusion
options.outcome: Forty minutes pass waiting for a central line with no vasoactive drug running. BP 76/40, CRT 4 s.

decisions.title: Communication with the parents
decisions.label: Your communication with the father
decisions.prompt: Her father stops you: “Is she going to die? I only gave her the syrup from the medical shop.”

opts.v: Find a quiet moment; tell him honestly she is very sick with an infection affecting her circulation
“She will be absolutely fine”
Explain what the team is doing and that she is going to the PICU
Keep him close to her where possible and tell him when he will get the next update
Ask what syrup and medicines she was given, and about allergies
“Why did you wait three days?”

options.text: Find a quiet moment; tell him honestly she is very sick with an infection affecting her circulation; Explain what the team is doing and that she is going to the PICU; Keep him close to her where possible and tell him when he will get the next update
options.outcome: He sits by her trolley holding her hand. He shows you the syrup — paracetamol — and says she has no allergies. He knows the doctor will speak to him after the PICU admission.
options.note: Be honest and kind, never falsely reassure, keep the parent close, and promise a time for the next update.

options.text: Some correct elements, nothing unsafe (partial)
options.outcome: He stands in the corridor not knowing what is happening, stopping staff to ask and pulling the team away from her.

options.text: “She will be absolutely fine”
options.outcome: When she is shifted to the PICU on an infusion he feels deceived and refuses consent until the consultant comes.

options.text: “Why did you wait three days?”
options.outcome: He goes silent and leaves the bay; the team loses the history of what she was given at home.

decisions.title: Team communication
decisions.label: Your communication with the team
decisions.prompt: The adrenaline infusion is about to start and the PICU must be told. How does the team communicate?

opts.v: Closed loop: repeat back drug, dose, dilution and rate before starting
“Start the adrenaline” — without saying the dose or rate
Name the roles: airway and monitor, IV and drugs, recorder
ISBAR to the PICU: 40 mL/kg given, antibiotic time, glucose, adrenaline rate and response
A second nurse checks the infusion and the pump
Hand over “septic child on adrenaline — rest is in the file”

options.text: Closed loop: repeat back drug, dose, dilution and rate before starting; Name the roles: airway and monitor, IV and drugs, recorder; ISBAR to the PICU: 40 mL/kg given, antibiotic time, glucose, adrenaline rate and response
options.outcome: “Adrenaline 0.1 microgram per kg per minute — running.” “Confirmed.” The recorder notes the time. The PICU registrar repeats back your ISBAR and has a bed and a pump ready.
options.note: Closed-loop orders, named roles and a structured handover prevent medication errors and lost information.

options.text: Some correct elements, nothing unsafe (partial)
options.outcome: The drug starts, but the PICU team arrive not knowing how much fluid she has had or when the antibiotic went in; time is lost re-checking.

options.text: “Start the adrenaline” — without saying the dose or rate
options.outcome: The infusion is started at ten times the intended rate. Within minutes HR 190, BP 140/90.

options.text: Hand over “septic child on adrenaline — rest is in the file”
options.outcome: In the PICU the antibiotic is nearly repeated and the fluid total is unknown; she is given a bolus she did not need. RR 40, SpO₂ 93 %.

decisions.title: Transfer
decisions.label: Your transfer plan
decisions.prompt: Meera needs intensive care. Where does she go, and how?

opts.v: PICU — in-house, or a tertiary PICU after stabilisation and a call ahead
Paediatric ward with 4-hourly observations
Doctor and nurse escort; monitor, oxygen, two working IV lines, adrenaline on a syringe pump with a spare syringe, resuscitation drugs
Before leaving: airway safe, BP and glucose rechecked, lines secured, records and consent with her
Her father travels with her
Stop the adrenaline for the transfer and restart it in the PICU

options.text: PICU — in-house, or a tertiary PICU after stabilisation and a call ahead; Doctor and nurse escort; monitor, oxygen, two working IV lines, adrenaline on a syringe pump with a spare syringe, resuscitation drugs; Before leaving: airway safe, BP and glucose rechecked, lines secured, records and consent with her
options.outcome: She leaves warm to the elbows on adrenaline, with you and the doctor beside her. In the PICU the bed, pump and team are ready.
options.note: Stabilise first, then move to the right place with the right team and kit; never interrupt a vasoactive infusion in transit.

options.text: Some correct elements, nothing unsafe (partial)
options.outcome: The move happens, but not every piece was in place; at the PICU door the spare syringe and her records are missing.

options.text: Paediatric ward with 4-hourly observations
options.outcome: On the ward at 3 am she is cold to the knees, BP 70/38, responding only to pain.

options.text: Stop the adrenaline for the transfer and restart it in the PICU
options.outcome: In the lift, off adrenaline, her BP falls to 64/32 and she becomes unresponsive.

debrief: Which PAT findings told you this was shock, and what made it life-threatening?
What did your first-five-minutes intervention include, and what do you check after every bolus?
What told you the shock was fluid-refractory, and why adrenaline in cold shock?

takeHome.t: Lethargy, mottling and cold peripheries = shock; hypotension (SBP below 70 + 2 × age) makes it decompensated.
First five minutes: oxygen, monitoring, IV/IO, glucose, culture, 20 mL/kg push–pull, antibiotic within the hour.
Reassess after every bolus; shock after 40–60 mL/kg is fluid-refractory — adrenaline in cold shock.
Honest and kind, never falsely reassure, keep the parent close, promise the next update.
Closed-loop drug orders, named roles, and an ISBAR handover with fluids, antibiotic time and drug rates.
Stabilise first; PICU with a doctor and nurse escort; never stop a vasoactive infusion in transit.

references: Surviving Sepsis Campaign International Guidelines for the Management of Septic Shock in Children (Weiss et al., 2020): fluid boluses, adrenaline/noradrenaline over dopamine, peripheral vasoactive infusion.
AHA PALS Provider Manual 2020: recognition of shock, hypotension thresholds, fluid resuscitation.
IAP ICC PCCN Module 03: types of shock, fluid resuscitation, NIBP.

ending.smooth: Meera reaches PICU warm to the elbows, passing urine, on adrenaline. She is weaned off the infusion on day 2.
ending.detour: Meera reaches PICU, but the time spent in shock means she needs ventilation and a longer course of vasoactive support.
